Crash Course Philosophy is brought to you
by Squarespace. Squarespace: share your passion with the world. In your day-to-day life, you probably assume
a whole bunch of different identities. You might be a sister to your brother, a daughter
to your parents, a colleague to your co-worker. A mentor to the kids you teach. Or you might think of your identity as being based on your interests, your skills, or things like your gender or ethnicity. Whatever they are, I’ll bet that you think
of your identities as being pretty fixed. Stable. And you like ‘em that way. And if that’s the case, I’d like you to meet this guy: 18th century Scottish philosopher David Hume. Because, he says you’re wrong. Hume argued that the idea of the self doesn’t
persist over time. He said there is no you that is the same person
from birth to death. He said the concept of the self is just an
illusion. This could be either liberating or terrifying,
depending on how you look at it. I mean, if you don’t have an identity, you
don’t have to worry about identity theft. But what does it mean for my understanding of myself, and for the people I love, if there is no single, constant me? If that’s the case, then the person I’m married to is literally not the person I fell in love with, or made those vows to. Which would suggest that I don’t need to
keep those vows, and neither does she. And what about personal responsibility? How can you hold someone accountable for their actions, if they’re not the same person now that they were before? And how can you be responsible for something
that you did, if you’re always changing? This is gonna get dicey. [Theme Music] If you joined me last time when we talked about personal identity, you’ll remember that we considered two main possibilities for what might preserve “you” as the same person over time. One approach was the body theory, the sort
of go-to view of things, which holds that you remain “you” over time, because you
just occupy the same body from birth to death. And the other was John Locke’s memory theory, the view that your memories are what makes you the same person over time: I’m me, because I remember being me in the
past. But both of these models have some problems. No matter how much we want the idea of permanent, persistent selves to be a thing, David Hume said that they just aren’t. For him, it was really a no-brainer. If having a certain identity means possessing
the same set of properties, he said, then how could anyone really maintain the same
identity from one moment to the next? I clearly don’t share all the same properties as my childhood self – or even my self before I shaved today – so Hume would say that it’s silly to pretend
I’m still me. But I feel like me.
So what did Hume think was going on? Hume said that the so-called “self” is just a bundle of impressions, consisting of a zillion different things – my body, my mind, emotions, preferences, memories,
even labels that are imposed on me by others. Think of a box – and say it’s marked “Hank” – and then put in that box everything that makes me who I am. My DNA, mannerisms, political leanings, my glasses, the relationships I have with others, the various roles I hold. Then, you take away the box. Hume’s point is, the “self” is just
shorthand for all the junk in the box. And the fact that there is no box points out that there’s no single underlying thing that holds it all together. And meanwhile, some of the stuff in the bundle
goes away, and new stuff shows up. So, if you look at the bundle that is me now,
and compare it with the bundle that my mom and dad brought home from the hospital, they would be almost completely different. So Hume said we’re all just ever-changing
bundles of impressions that our minds are fooled into thinking of as constant, because they’re packaged in these fleshy receptacles that basically look the same from one day to the next. To explore this some more, let’s bounce over to the Thought Bubble for some Flash Philosophy. Contemporary British philosopher Derek Parfit, probably after watching a Star Trek marathon, posed this thought experiment. Imagine a machine that breaks you down atom-by-atom, copies all of that information, and transmits it to Mars, at the speed of light. Once that information gets to Mars, another machine uses it to re-create you, atom by atom, using copies of the same organic stuff that
you were composed of here on earth. The person who wakes up on Mars has all the same memories and personality as you did – and that person thinks it’s you. So here’s the question – is this space
travel? Did you travel to Mars? Is the transported person really you? Or was a new being created that just happens to correspond to you, atom by atom, thought by thought? Now, consider this: What if a new version of the machine is created, so that now, instead of destroying your body, it can simply be scanned, and all the information can be re-created on Mars, but the you here on earth still exists. Now did you travel?
Or were you just replicated? If you’re here on earth, are you also on
Mars? Wow…uh, yeah, thanks, Thought Bubble…
I think. Parfit agrees with Hume that there isn’t
such a thing as personal identity over time. So, he says, in either case, you didn’t
travel through space – that’s just a new you that shows up on Mars, whether the old you was destroyed or still exists. And you know what? Even if you hopped on a spaceship and flew to Mars the old-fashioned way, it’d still be a new you that arrives, because you would’ve experienced all sorts
of changes during the trip. But the thing is, Parfit thought Hume missed
a really important point.

Crash Course Philosophy presents an overview of personal identity as proposed by 18th century Scottish philosopher David Hume.

**Hume's Argument:** Hume challenged the notion that a self remains unchanging throughout life.  He argued that identity is an illusion based on the idea of "impressions", a bundle of physical components and mental processes, constantly changing over time. This contradicts the common idea of a persistent "you."

**Challenges to Identity Theory:** Hume's perspective was challenged by both body theory (permanent bodily existence) and memory theory (continuity through past memories).  Hume ultimately deemed them invalid: "If having a certain identity means possessing the same set of properties, he said, then how could anyone really maintain the same identity from one moment to the next?"

**Derek Parfit's Thought Experiments:** Modern philosopher Derek Parfit added a twist to the discussion. In his thought experiment where information is transmitted across space and reassembled on Mars,  new being on earth results with identical memories and personality, creating a duplicate of an individual.  He poses philosophical questions regarding "being" and "identity."

**Parfit's Conclusion:** Parfit agrees with Hume that there isn’t consistent personal identity over time. In either scenario—destruction and re-creation or merely transferring information—the result is a new being, not the person who went on "travel".
 
**Hume's Perspective:**  Despite considering an intriguing perspective, David Hume missed something crucial according to Parfit.

###  The Enduring Nature of Personal Identity 

This transcript explores the concept of personal identity and the philosophical challenges it presents. 

**David Hume's View:** 

- Hume argues that the enduring self is an impossible concept. He challenged the notion of a constant, persistent personality by examining the ever-changing nature of our experiences and physical selves.
- According to his theory, our identities are more like bundles of impressions – constantly shifting as memories emerge, emotions change, and experiences take place - than singular, unchanging entities.

**Derek Parfit's Thought Experiment:**

- Imagine human transport:  information about a person's entire being is transported from Earth to Mars. Another machine then copies this information and creates a new individual on the red planet.
- The thought experiment explores whether transporting an identical copy constitutes travel, suggesting a parallel existence rather than relocation within time-space dimensions.

**Parfit's Consideration of Psychological Connection:**  

Parfit aligns with Hume in his rejection of the idea of a singular, enduring self but offers different insights.
 - He suggests that our identities are like chainmail, comprised of numerous interconnected links representing experiences and memories over time – thus contributing to a greater 'identity' structure.
- Parfit proposes that these links intertwine, some lasting for long periods while others fade away (like personal tastes); this process underscores the enduring nature of certain aspects of self.

**Continuous Transformation:** 

Even if someone travelled to Mars on their trip and arrived with a new perspective – they would still be undergoing continuous transformation as time progressed.

David Hume argued that personal identity across time wasn't possible. He claimed the idea of a constant "self" was flawed because it didn't align with how our physical and psychological attributes changed.

Hume described the "self" as a collection of impressions, including our body, thoughts, emotions, preferences, memories, even labels imposed by others. These impressions make up a package that represents our identity, with the fact there's no singular underlying structure demonstrating a lack of a fixed self over time.

Philosopher Derek Parfit further examined this question through a thought experiment: Imagine transferring our "consciousness" to Mars, atom-by-atom. This would produce a new person on Mars who possesses identical memory and personality traits to the original individual. Is this "travel"? 

Both Hume and Parfit agreed on one key point - time doesn't create an immutable sense of self because constant change is inevitable in our lives. Yet, they differed slightly when considering subjective consciousness as it relates to personal identity. 

Parfit viewed psychological connections within our personal lives as crucial elements, creating a chainmail-like structure for our identities. As we experience life, new links are created while other pre-existing ones naturally recede into the past due to disconnection and change. These interconnected experiences shape our identities and how we perceive ourselves over time; even with fundamental transitions in our self.

David Hume said that permanent, persistent selves can't exist. For him, having an identity means possessing the same set of properties, which is impossible across moments. He felt it's nonsensical to pretend I'm still the same person as before, considering how my characteristics have evolved compared to my past self, or even a moment ago. 

So, what did Hume theorize?  Hume described the "self" as a bundle of impressions including things like my body, mind, emotions, preferences, memories, and labels imposed on me by others. Imagine a box with your defining elements within—like your DNA, mannerisms, political leanings, eyeglasses, relationships, and roles—and then removes the box. Hume's point is this: the "self" is merely shorthand for all components of me in the box, emphasizing there is no single underlying factor binding everything together; plus, some components vanish while new ones appear. 

So when comparing two “bundles” – one from my childhood and another today – they would be dramatically different. In Hume's estimation, we are constantly changing bundles of impressions that our minds misinterpret as constant because they're packaged in those temporary forms that look largely same across time. To understand this more deeply, let's delve into the Thought Bubble for some Flash Philosophy. 

Derek Parfit, probably inspired by a Star Trek marathon, posed a thought experiment: Imagine a tech capable of breaking down our physical bodies, copying all bodily data to Mars at light speed. After transfer, another machine replicates you atom-by-atom on Mars using copies of the stuff that constituted your human form here on earth. Upon reaching Mars, this individual's memories and personality are identical to yours, but also believes themselves to have achieved a new state of being. Now, what if there's no transport, yet still remains "transport"? Is it actual travel or just replica-based relocation? Are the transported individuals us? 

Another question that arises: What if we reimagine that this tech, that instead of destroying our physical forms, merely creates a scan, with all required data transferred to Mars for replication. But now, on Earth, your "self" is still present!  Was I really transported to Mars, or just replicated? If you're on earth today, were you also there yesterday? Wow...uh, yeah thanks Thought Bubble… 

I believe Parfit agrees with Hume: There's no concept of true personal identity throughout time. In either case, we didn't undergo this journey in space - an entirely new person arises on Mars due to the transformation and process described. As I move further down the timeline of my existence, links get created which contribute to a greater network that connects each link to a certain sequence of events. Some links are constantly being formed and reinforced. For example, my shift away from Dora the Explorer indicates that a connection to childhood had disappeared. Likewise, discovering a more profound love for philosophy triggered growth. Some chains intersect with other existing links and will continue to exist through time. Parfit's theory on identity highlights  that individual selves are not static entities. While physical matter undergoes substantial change, psychological connections between individuals persist over time. 

He proposes a model comparing identities to chainmail, where interconnected experiences shape the self: new links are formed as time passes; older links drop off based on psychological disconnection. This process leads to continuous change and adaptation with the self's essence undergoing significant transformations. Parfit argues that even though changes in physical matter occur over time (like at birth), enduring psychological connections, linking back to previous selves, contribute to a sense of personal continuity—though not in an unchanging form. He defines "survival" as remaining connected to past experiences, ensuring relevance during the passage of time.

Parfit asserts that change is inevitable; he offers insight into how humans react and adapt when encountering former individuals: "Catching up with an old friend requires a first acknowledgment of changes over time." Recognizing and adapting to these transformations facilitates connection: just as we re-acquaint ourselves with familiar figures, understanding the evolution of the self's character, as well as others', is essential for meaningful relationships. 

In terms of obligations and responsibilities, Parfit clarifies that individuals should consider these in light of their personal connections—not a rigid adherence to pre-defined boundaries or outdated ideals.  If one's actions diverge drastically over time, like transitioning from a bully to a kind individual, they shouldn bear no responsibility for past offenses. 

Similarly, re: "promises" such as marriage vows: Parfit proposes that vows should not be viewed through the lens of static identity. As individuals evolve throughout a lifetime, their sense of commitment adapts too—marriage is interpreted not as an obligation rooted in the past self but the present reality. With evolution and change inherent to human existence, he advocates for adapting and re-negotiating those vows during changing realities.

Finally, this approach highlights what is truly "relevant" about promises: promises are reassessed, renegotiated, and revisited with new challenges as personal narratives evolve - each interaction becomes a reflection on individual growth, shared experiences, and mutual understanding with time.
clean_text: "Even though there isn’t a singular 'you' from birth to death, Parfit says that each of us has a psychological connectedness with ourselves over time. Think about your life as being like a piece of chainmail. The mesh that makes up your personal identity is made up of lots of separate chains, and those chains intersect at certain points, to make up the chain mail. As you follow the timeline of one particular set of links, new links are being created that add to the chain. And as time passes, the links that are farther back in your past slowly start to drop off, as they lose their psychological connection to you. So, when you stopped loving Dora the Explorer, that link dropped away. And when you discovered that you totally love philosophy, a new link was created. But some chains intersect with that other chain, and they have links that persist for a long time, like the love you have for your parents. So Parfit says that, sure, I’m not the same person that I was in elementary school. And I won't be the same person when I die. I’m not even really the same person I was when I started this sentence because every experience changes us, at least a little. But parts of me survive the passage of time, because they’re psychologically connected to my previous selves. And survival is what’s important for Parfit. As long as enough of the elements you persist, you see yourself as relevantly the same. But not for a whole lifetime.  Parfit would say none of the 'you' that existed at birth is still around—your physical matter is almost all different, and you have no memory of that time, and your preferences have completely changed. Baby You hasn’t survived.  But some Last Year You probably has. And Parfit seems to have hit on an important insight here. Think about what you do when you catch up with an old friend. The first thing you do is ask what's happened since you last spoke. What you're doing, without really thinking about it, is recognizing that you both have changed. If the changes are big, then your friend could seem like a stranger at first. So, when it’s someone you care about, you take the time to reacquaint yourself with this new person. Because, you recognize the need to always know the most updated version of that person. But the opposite can also happen. Think about that aunt you only see at Christmas, who still pinches your cheek and gives you a new American Girl doll every year. She probably knew what you loved when you were 10. But she doesn’t know the current you. The version of you she’s shopping for at Christmas doesn't exist anymore.  But since you rarely see each other, and you haven’t made the effort to know the new yous, you're both looking past each other in that painfully awkward way in that makes holidays with relatives so special. So now let’s think back to the question we discussed earlier—if I’m not the same me over time, how do I know them and be close to them over time? Today we continued our exploration of personal identity, learning about Hume’s bundle theory and Parfit's theory of survival through psychological connectedness.
